title: Google's ADK + MCP = The Future of AI Agents
transcriptText:
[MUSIC PLAYING]
HEMANTH HM: Hi, I'm Hemanth.
I'm a senior engineering manager
at PayPal, leading AI labs.
And I am here at
DevFest Silicon Valley.
And with me is Smitha.
SMITHA KOLAN: Hi, I'm Smitha,
and I'm a senior developer
relations here at Google Cloud.
HEMANTH HM: Great to have
you here in the show, Smitha.
We start off with this
classic question--
what is your
definition of an agent?
SMITHA KOLAN: That's
a great question.
I feel like everyone has
their own definition,
but for me specifically, I
would say that an AI agent is
a system that uses a model
to reason about any task
that you give it
in order to select
the right tools to
complete that task.
HEMANTH HM: Nice, yeah.
I like the way you said
"reason," and "task,"
and "tools."
This summarizes a good
definition of what an agent is.
And you are also
into the ADK world.
Tell us more about
what ADK is, and why
is it useful for our audience?
And we can get a
bit deeper into it.
SMITHA KOLAN: Yeah, absolutely.
ADK is an open-source
Agent Development Kit.
It's a framework for
helping developers
build agentic systems.
It's amazing.
It's also really easy
and developer friendly
in order to deploy.
It's great when you want to do
stuff like evaluating agents.
It also has a lot
of great endpoints.
So, for example,
you can connect it
with open-source tools
like OpenAI, any sorts
of open-source tools out there.
It also comes with something
called the MCP toolset, which
I'm actually a huge fan
of, which allows you
to connect with MCP servers.
And that's how
models communicate
with external environments.
HEMANTH HM: So you're saying
it's kind of a complete package,
which kind of helps you to have
a set of tools which is probably
defined within the
local scope, or maybe
talk to an MPP, remote or local,
and do all the orchestration
that's needed.
SMITHA KOLAN: Yes, exactly.
HEMANTH HM: So if you were
to see one of the challenges
that ADK is trying to
solve today, what is it?
What's the top in the list
that needs to be solved?
And can the industry
as a whole on the
free-- because it's
free and open source,
as you said-- can all of the
contributors come into one room
and discuss, and
brainstorm, and try
to change the direction
at which it's heading?
SMITHA KOLAN: Yeah, absolutely.
In my opinion, I think one
of the biggest things which
ADK is actually trying to
solve is make it easier
for developers to build agents.
And that's the
single biggest thing
that it's trying
to solve because--
think about it.
This is a very nascent space.
How many frameworks are there
out there which you can actually
build agents with in a super
easy and deployable way?
And that's exactly
the main thing
that ADK is trying to solve.
And also, the fact that
you can code with it
in multiple languages helps.
It's really friendly
for developers to use.
HEMANTH HM: Does it
also mean that there
is some kind of a tight
coupling with Google infra?
Is that the case with ADK?
Or you say, hey, ADK
is agnostic of whatever
cloud layer that you have,
it's easy to deploy and run?
Is that where we are
getting, or is there
some kind of an coupling with
Google's Cloud infrastructure?
SMITHA KOLAN: So ADK is
not only model agnostic.
It's also cloud agnostic.
You can think of it that way.
But if you really want to
deploy to Google's amazing cloud
services, you can
easily do that.
It's like a one-step
command, especially
for things like Cloud Run.
Cloud Run is one
of the best places
that you can actually deploy
AI agents with, especially
if you've built them with ADK.
It's a one-step command
in order to do that.
There's a multitude
of ways that you
can go about deploying your
agents on Google Cloud,
and ADK has all the
compatibilities.
HEMANTH HM: Yeah, that's great.
Switching gears
a bit, let's talk
about agent-first development.
What I mean by
agent-first development
is an agent being
kind of a companion
throughout the
software-development lifecycle,
not just in terms of
developing code, or deploying,
and monitoring, or
testing and such
but also, before even you
start a project, when you're
sitting in a room
and brainstorming
with your product, and design,
and all the engineering,
and machine learning, and data
scientists, everybody in a room,
and we are discussing
an idea, I would
see an agent sitting
there and helping
us to nudge, ask
questions, and participate
to product and designers
kind of doing a prototype
and then the engineering
taking it to production.
So I kind of sense and see
agents sitting everywhere here.
So agent-first is more of a
paradigm where two parts here--
one while you're developing.
You have agents who are helping.
And second, you're also
kind of building for agents.
You're not just
building for humans.
You're also saying-- A2A
is a classic example.
You're building for agents,
and you're thinking agent
as the first-class citizen.
So what do you feel
about this paradigm,
and how do you also see
ADK fitting in here,
or what's been your
experience in this patch?

exactly how you set it.
You can use agents
in every aspect
of that software-development
lifecycle.
It's not just about,
hey, I'm going
to be white coding with my
agent and building this app out.
You can also brainstorm
with your agent.
One of the most classic
examples with ADK
is actually building
researcher agents,
and that can help with
prototyping an app before you
actually start building it.
Even writing design
docs, so stuff like that
are what agents are
really great for.
And I think one of the
best things about building
agents in this system,
or in this new age,
is actually building them
purpose-built, so not
multipurpose agents but actually
for a very specific purpose,
for example, writing design docs
or doing testing of software.
So yeah, there's a
ton that you could do.
HEMANTH HM: Great, yeah.
And you've also been
an educator, right?
SMITHA KOLAN: Yeah.
HEMANTH HM: What do you think
that the younger generation
should start learning?
Of course, they have to learn
to solve problems and things
to think, maybe meta
thinking and such,
but even that AI has kind
of drastically changed
on ways of learning.
Where do you think the younger
generation should focus on,
and how should they learn?

at a talk yesterday.
It was actually here
on the Google campus,
and they were talking
about how, when,
initially, when web
frameworks came out,
people were talking
about how, oh my god, we
won't need developers anymore.

comes out, and you're
able to code really
easily, people think,
oh, we might not need
software developers anymore,
and it's going to be extinct.

We've went through
multiple cycles of this
over the last three decades.

it's more important now
to learn AI than ever before.
It's also more
important now to learn
how to code than ever before.
So, I think, for the
younger generation,
that's the biggest takeaway.
And the things that we've heard
in the past, it is to go deep.
But also, I think
it's really important
to go broad and be kind of
an expert in many things.

We saw this over the three
decades, as you said,
maybe even when
computers came in
and all the typewriters
were replaced.
People said, oh, everyone's
going to lose their job.
And maybe even-- predating
when calculators came in,
same thing happened.
So this keeps repeating
over the years.
But I feel with AI, there's
a bit of a greater tangent
to how we were solving things.
And if you're good at your
art, it kind of accelerates
the process.
So I give this analogy saying
that, hey, my handwriting is
good or I take a
good photograph.

it's just because
of the pen or the camera.

but it's about the time
that I have spent in
specializing this art.
So I feel programming is also
kind of an art in itself.
SMITHA KOLAN: Exactly.
And it's evolving day
by day, month by month.
So it's more important now
than ever to learn how to code
and also to learn how AI works.
HEMANTH HM: Absolutely.

favorite question--
I keep asking this in
multiple interviews--
is, as AI is kind of
advancing, probably
we might reach a
state where you don't
have to use your neural
capacity to remember things.

sitting with you.

in your brain,
and you're going to
asynchronously passing tasks,
and it's going to
handle or probably--
I was joking the other day
saying that you think and shop
or you record your
dreams and play back.
We might reach there
in the coming decades.

that we, as humans,
being dependent on these
tools for assistance,
or maybe as a companion,
are we losing our intuition?

that's necessarily the case.
And this is not a
general statement,
but I feel like
AI actually helps
you focus more and do things
that you actually want to do.
It helps you get
rid of tasks which
you don't want to do and focus
on things that you actually
doing.
And that's what,
I believe, AI is
being used for across
the space by developers.
I know personally they
use AI to offload tasks
that they don't like
doing so that they
can focus more and do things
that they actually doing.

The things that we like to
do, we should do that more,
and maybe assistants
can take that overhead.
But sometimes, it comes back
with a lot of confidence,
even though it's hallucinating.
And that's where we need the
human in the loop to say,
you know what, you're wrong.
Or you probably nudged AI to
go in the right direction.
So that's where we
are as we stand.

AGI is coming soon,
and what is your
definition of AGI?

If you look 20 years ago, the
models right now that we have--

them 20 years ago,
you would think this is AGI.

focusing on when AGI is coming,
we should look at what's
capable right now, which
is, we're at a really
unique time in the space
where purpose-built artificial
intelligence is already here,
for example,
software-development
agents, testing agents.

think, is actually really
exciting about this space.

really interesting.
As I said, if AGI is
a moving goal post,
that means we already
have AGI, in a way.
SMITHA KOLAN: If you
look 20 years ago, yeah.

one really thought

developing code or monitoring
deployments and stuff.
SMITHA KOLAN: Exactly.

here two school of thoughts.

of school of thought.

change the direction

many schools of thought on this,

like AI is a bubble.

transformed people's lives.

that's inherently

we're in a bubble right now.

it because everyone's

with tools.

models behaving like agents,

models getting better,

how agents and models

compound more and more.

super excited about.

how the industry is evolving.

forward for the future,

your predictions and see.

for being here, Smitha.
It was a great conversation.
SMITHA KOLAN: It was
great talking with you.
